Denise, before the slides. In twenty years I have sat through two kinds of post-mortem: one that explains a quarter and one that apologises for it. Which am I about to hear?
The first. Three things: what we missed, why we missed it, and what changes in October.
Then start with the warning sign. Was there one, or are we discussing something that nobody in this building could have seen?

There was one, and we saw it. Submissions in the industrial book fell in June. We read it as a near miss repeating itself, and we should have tested that reading instead of explaining it. In retrospect, the pressure must have been building since March.
Careful with should have. Once, it is accountability. Five times, it is a confession, and this room stops listening at three. Tell me instead what you could have done and chose not to.

We could have re-priced the two largest accounts in July. We decided not to, in a room, with the numbers in front of us. That was a judgment call, not an oversight, and I would like the board to hear the difference.
So would I. Most reviews treat the two identically, and they are not the same failure at all. What was the blind spot?

Assuming the renewal cycle would behave as it did last year. That is the root cause, not the June number. Nobody owned that assumption, which is precisely why nobody tested it. The corrective action is a monthly re-pricing review from October, with my name against it. It might have saved two of the four points we lost. I cannot claim more than that.
That I can take to the board. A room forgives a quarter far faster than it forgives ten minutes of apologising for one.
We could have re-priced in July, and we chose not to.
That was a judgment call, not an oversight.
It might have saved two of the four points. I cannot claim more than that.

I ran reviews for eleven years, and almost all of the bad ones fail in the same place. They start with who, and the who arrives before the what. Once a name is on the table, everybody in the room is defending something, and the analysis is over. The good ones invert it. They rebuild the timeline first, what was known on the fourteenth of June and by whom, before anybody is allowed to say what should have happened. Hindsight makes the signal look enormous. At the time it was one line in a report of forty. The second thing I watch for is the language. If somebody tells me the market must have shifted, I ask what would be true if it had. If they cannot answer, they are not deducing, they are decorating. And the last rule is mine. A review that ends without a date and a name has not ended. It has been postponed.

There is a version of accountability that is really just anxiety, and I did it for years. I would open a review by listing everything I should have done, on the theory that if I said it first, nobody else could say it to me. It works exactly once. After that the room does not hear ownership. It hears somebody who cannot stop apologising, and quietly it stops giving that person difficult work to do. What changed it for me was one line from a chairman. Say it once, say it in the past, and then talk about October. One sentence of should have, and everything after that in the future. The other habit I had to lose was second-guessing in public, reopening the same decision three times in one meeting. In retrospect is a useful phrase. Said four times in ten minutes, it is a person negotiating with the past in front of an audience.

Revenue closed four points below plan, and the shortfall sits almost entirely in the industrial book. The warning sign was there in June, and the pressure must have been building since March. The root cause was an assumption about the renewal cycle that nobody owned, so nobody tested it. From October we re-price the twenty largest accounts every month, and that review has my name against it.
